Fortitude

/FOR-ti-tood/ — rhymes with latitude · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Fortitude is the inner strength and courage that allows a person to endure pain, hardship, or difficulty without giving up.

It took real fortitude to finish the race on a sprained ankle.

Worked Example

Running the entire marathon on a badly sprained ankle, the runner refused to stop, pushing through searing pain mile after mile.

Fortitude is more precise than 'courage' because it names the specific inner strength needed to endure prolonged pain or hardship without giving up. Courage is momentary bravery; fortitude is sustained strength through suffering.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

courage: bravery when facing fear or danger

grit: toughness that keeps you going long-term

perseverance: steady persistence despite setbacks and delays

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

weakness: lack of strength to endure difficulty

cowardice: shameful lack of courage under hardship

Where it sits · how unbreakable the inner strength — courage → fortitude → resilience → indomitable

courage vs. fortitude: Courage is the base that fortitude builds on: courage faces one frightening moment, while fortitude endures pain or hardship steadily over a long time.

resilience vs. fortitude: Resilience sits a notch above fortitude on this scale: fortitude is the strength to endure hardship without giving up, while resilience adds springing back from it fully.

indomitable vs. fortitude: Indomitable is the top of the scale, beyond fortitude: fortitude endures hardship without complaint, but an indomitable spirit cannot be conquered by anything at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — fort

Root — fort: strong, brave (from fortis) (Latin)

Suffix — -itude

Suffix — -itude: state or quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin fortis ('strong') plus -itude ('state of'), fortitude is literally 'the state of being strong' — the inner strength and courage to endure pain or hardship without giving up.

Use the root in a new word: fortify

Use the root in a new word: fortify: Soldiers fortify a camp to make it strong against attack — the same Latin root fortis, 'strong,' that gives fortitude its meaning of inner strength.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Fortitude is more elevated and literary than everyday words like 'strength' or 'courage.' It suggests a kind of moral dignity and noble perseverance. Use it when you want to describe someone's dignified, sustained strength through real difficulty or pain. For simple toughness, the plainer words are better.
